SK0230 The object initializer is empty

A pair of object or collection initializer braces that sets nothing: new Foo { } is new Foo(). An empty with is a copy, and is never reported.

CategoryCleanup
Default severitywarning
ScopeSyntax
Needs a compilationno
Runs under --load=looseyes
Cached per fileyes
Fixyes, review it
Language version floor—
Since2.0

Why

Empty braces read as a list somebody is about to fill in and stay in the file for years after nobody is. new Foo { } is two characters of ceremony over new Foo(), and the constructor call is all either of them performs.

⚠ `x with { }` used to be this rule's too, and it is not redundant (#636). It was read as a record copy that changes nothing and fixed to x. But the copy is the change: with on a record class calls the copy constructor and returns a distinct instance, so the fix aliased a clone the author made in order to keep it apart. Measured on Vixen, where it removed four: an extracted texture layer went on sharing its instance with the stack it came from, a palette test compared an object with itself, and two equality tests stopped testing anything. An empty with is the one way C# spells "a copy of this", so this rule no longer looks at with at all.

Example

Instead of:

var options = new JsonSerializerOptions { };
var buffer = new List<byte> { };

Write:

var options = new JsonSerializerOptions();
var buffer = new List<byte>();

When it does not fire

⚠ An empty `with` is never reported, on anything `with` applies to. On a record class the copy is a distinct instance, made by a copy constructor that can be written by hand and do anything. On a struct, a record struct or an anonymous type the copy is a value, and it is still not the operand: (s with { }).Mutate() mutates a temporary where s.Mutate() mutates s, and an anonymous instance is a reference that ReferenceEquals can tell apart. ⚠ The fix is still declared unsafe without the `with`, and expression trees are the reason. Compiled code cannot tell new Foo { } from new Foo(), but inside a lambda converted to Expression<…> the first is a MemberInitExpression with no bindings and the second a NewExpression, and a query provider is free to translate the two differently. ⚠ Only the two initializer kinds that mean "and then set these members" are matched. An empty array initializer belongs to an ArrayCreationExpression, which this rule never sees — new int[] { } cannot lose its braces and still compile. An anonymous type is a different node again: new { } has no new () to become. ⚠ A creation with no argument list grows one, because new Foo is not an expression; a creation that already has arguments keeps them, and new() target-typed creation is matched through the same path. ⚠ A comment or a preprocessor directive between the braces withdraws the finding: an empty initializer holding a note is a note about why it is empty, and the fix deletes the braces wholesale.
